title: Purl chipping
subtitle: Tiny cut lengths of bright check purl sewn on like beads to scatter sparkle across a surface
excerpt: Purl chipping cuts bright check purl, a hollow coiled metal thread, into short chip lengths and sews each one flat against the fabric through its hollow centre. The chips catch the light from many angles and give a faceted, glittering fill to goldwork shapes.
sourceNotes: Barbara Dawson, Metal Thread Embroidery (1968), purl and chipping chapter. Royal School of Needlework standard goldwork curriculum. Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882), purl entries.

glossaryTerms.definition: A hollow coiled metal thread with a faceted, angular cut to its wire, so it reflects light from multiple directions. It is cut into short lengths called chips and sewn on like beads.
A small pad covered with velvet used in goldwork to hold cut purl chips without them rolling away. The pile grips the metal coils while you pick them up one at a time.

content.text: Purl chipping covers a goldwork shape with tiny metal chips that scatter light across the surface.

is a hollow coiled wire with a faceted surface. Cutting it into lengths of 2 to 4 mm produces chips that can be threaded on a needle and sewn flat to the fabric, each one sitting like a short bead. Because the chips are cut at slightly different lengths and laid in varying directions, the finished area glitters rather than reflecting as a single plane.

items.label: Metal thread
items.value: Bright check purl, size 6 or 8; smooth purl or rough purl can be mixed in for texture variation

items.label: Couching thread
items.value: Fine waxed yellow or gold silk thread, one strand; beeswax the thread before use

items.label: Ground
items.value: Firm silk or linen over a felt padding layer, mounted on a slate frame

items.label: Needle
items.value: Fine sharps needle size 10 or 12; sharp point needed to pass through the fabric alongside each chip

content.text: Cut the purl into chips on a
using small sharp scissors. Make each chip roughly 2 to 3 mm long. Cut only a small quantity at a time; purl chips roll easily and the velvet pile holds them in place.
Thread the fine needle with a single strand of waxed silk. Bring the needle up through the fabric at one corner of the area being filled.

Pick up one chip by sliding the needle through its hollow centre. Hold the chip against the fabric and insert the needle back down into the fabric at the far end of the chip, so the chip lies flat like a bead with the thread passing through it.

Continue across the area, placing chips close together and varying their angle slightly so no two adjacent chips run in exactly the same direction. Leave gaps no larger than the width of one chip between them.
At the edge of the shape, trim any chip that would extend beyond the outline rather than forcing it to bend. A bent chip will dull and lose its sparkle.

items.symptom: Chips stand upright rather than lying flat
items.cause: The chip is longer than the stitch length, or the entry and exit holes are placed too close together.
items.fix: The distance between where the needle comes up and where it goes back down must match the cut length of the chip. Adjust the chip length or the stitch placement.

items.symptom: The thread shows between chips and the surface looks sparse
items.cause: Chips placed too far apart, or the thread is a contrasting colour.
items.fix: Place chips edge to edge so no gap is visible. Use a matching gold or yellow silk so any tiny gap is not obvious.

items.symptom: The purl tarnishes or looks dull on the finished piece
items.cause: Purl was handled with bare hands during cutting and stitching.
items.fix: Handle purl with clean dry fingers or fine tweezers. The oils in skin tarnish the metal surface quickly.
